catholic-encyclopedia-1913-joseph-albert:
Joseph Albert Alberdingk Thijm was a Dutch Catholic writer who shaped his country's Catholic revival in the nineteenth century. Born at Amsterdam in 1820, he began in commerce but broke into print as an art critic in 1842. Poet, philologist, and critic at once, he edited the periodical Dietsche Warande for three decades and wrote verse ranked among the best Dutch poetry of his age.

Thijm defended Catholic art and history against every attacker, taking Nil nisi per Christum, nothing except through Christ, as his motto. His 1852 memorial to Rome helped restore the Catholic hierarchy in the Netherlands with Utrecht as archiepiscopal see. His last work was a complete edition of the poet Vondel, whom he admired above all.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-peter-paul-ma:
Paul Alberdingk Thijm was a Dutch literary historian, born at Amsterdam in 1827. He studied at the Gymnasium and Athenaeum of his home city, graduating in letters and history in 1857, then taught history at Maastricht. Called to Louvain in 1870, he founded a chair for the special study of Dutch literature and spent his career reviving the Flemish spirit at the university.

Less gifted than his elder brother Joseph, he shared his enthusiasm for literature and art and championed the Christian ideal in art with ready zeal. He presided over the associations Tijd en Vlijt and Constantius Buter, joined the Flemish Academy and presided over it for a time, and from 1888 edited Dietsche Warande, carrying it into Belgium. His books range from St. Willibrord and Charlemagne to a prize-winning survey of Belgian charity. He died at Louvain in 1904.
podcast-dannyjones-T3joytzJDjM:
Danny Jones uses this episode to come clean, in the title's phrase, on the moon debate: his own shifting position on whether the Apollo landings happened as NASA says. His co-guest Matt Cox, the former con man and storyteller, nearly walks off the show as the argument heats up, and that friction becomes the episode's second act.

Jones has hosted landing believers and deniers alike, and here he must finally referee his own archive. Cox brings a fraudster's nose for a staged story, applied in an unexpected direction. Nothing in the episode settles the moon question, which the evidence elsewhere settles thoroughly; what it settles is where this show stands, in public, after platforming every side. Listeners get a rare thing in podcasting: a host auditing his own catalog, with a friend threatening to leave over the verdict.
podcast-joerogan-vDEsV0AhcjM:
Handwashing, and the fight to make doctors practice it, anchors this Joe Rogan Experience segment. In the 1840s, Ignaz Semmelweis showed that clean hands saved mothers in his Vienna maternity ward. Instead of thanks, the medical establishment mocked and ruined him.

Rogan and his guest use that story to judge how medicine treats new ideas that shame old habits. They note that Semmelweis had data but no germ theory to explain it, so pride won. The talk then turns to modern cases of experts resisting obvious fixes. It is a warning about pride dressed up as science.
